modern: From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and unwavering steadiness of purpose; and to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except reason; and to be always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, and in long illness; and to see clearly in a living example that the same man can be both most resolute and yielding, and not irritable in giving his instruction; and to have had before my eyes a man who clearly regarded his experience and his skill in explaining philosophical principles as the least of his merits; and from him I learned how to receive from friends what are regarded as favours, without being either humbled by them or letting them pass unnoticed.
original: From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and undeviating steadiness of purpose; and to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except to reason; and to be always the same, in sharp pains, on the occasion of the loss of a child, and in long illness; and to see clearly in a living example that the same man can be both most resolute and yielding, and not peevish in giving his instruction; and to have had before my eyes a man who clearly considered his experience and his skill in expounding philosophical principles as the smallest of his merits; and from him I learned how to receive from friends what are esteemed favors, without being either humbled by them or letting them pass unnoticed.

explained.summary:
Apollonius, one of his Stoic teachers, showed Marcus how to rely on his own reason and stay the same person through pain, illness and even the death of a child. He was both firm and gentle, patient when teaching, and treated his great skill as the least of his qualities.

He also showed how to accept favours from friends gracefully: without feeling smaller for it, and without pretending it didn’t happen.
